title: Mara comes
hookLine: Mara with his bow of flowers and his army of horrors (Buddhacarita 13)

cards: Flowers on the bow. Flowers on the arrows. The figure who comes for the prince doesn't look like a monster at first.

He looks like desire itself, and that's who he is. The prince has eaten, bathed, and walked to a great tree, and he has sat down beneath it, resolved not to get up until he has found what he's looking for.
The poem says the whole world grew glad at that. Except one. In his own realm, Mara trembles.

teach.h: THE GOD OF LOVE, THE ENEMY OF FREEDOM.
teach.b: First, who Mara is. The poem gives him two names at once. In the world he is called the god of love, the one with the flowered bow.
And he is also Mara, the enemy of freedom. Ashvaghosha joins them on purpose: the one who makes us want and the one who keeps us bound are, in this poem, the same figure. Second, his fear.
His sons and daughters ask why he's troubled. That man under the tree, he says, has put on the armor of resolve.

teach.h: IF HE WINS, MY REALM IS EMPTY.
teach.b: If he wins, he'll lead others out of my realm, and it will stand empty. So I'll break his vow before he finishes. Third, the bow.
Mara goes to the tree with his children and speaks first. Get up, he says, in paraphrase. You're a warrior by birth.
Go back to your duty, rule, make offerings, win heaven the proper way. Give up this begging road.
If you won't rise, here's my arrow. He lets it fly. The prince doesn't stir.
He doesn't even seem to notice it. Fourth, the army. Mara is shaken, and changes weapons: if desire won't work, fear might.

He calls up his army, and the poem fills the air around the tree with horrors, creatures with the faces of beasts, many-armed, many-headed, carrying spears, clubs, swords and burning trees, howling, surrounding the seated man on every side.
That's where the poem leaves him today. Notice the order of attack. The soft weapon first: the appeal to duty, to sense, to pleasure.
Only when the flower arrow fails does Mara reach for the horrors.

how: Mara's attack on the seated Buddha is painted and carved in Buddhist art, and some Buddhist teachers speak of Mara as a name for whatever in the mind pulls a person away from awakening.

o: a god arrives to bless the prince's vow
a demon comes to punish the prince's sins
the tempter arrives to break the prince's resolve

games.q: Mara under the tree: tap the pairs.
p: the name Mara has in the world
go back to a warrior's duty

s: in the poem, Mara attacks first with his army of horrors
he tries the flower bow and a speech about duty first; the army comes after.
the poem links Mara with the god of love
it calls him the god of love in the world, and the enemy of freedom.
the poem says he doesn't stir, and doesn't even seem to notice it.

games.q: you're seated beneath a tree, resolved not to rise. a figure with a bow of flowers tells you to get up and go back to your duty, and draws an arrow. what do you do?
o: get up and argue with him.
games.why: the prince doesn't stir. the arrow flies and does nothing, so Mara changes weapons and calls up his army of horrors.

practice: Let the body be as still as you comfortably can, like someone seated beneath a tree, and let one fear come forward, not the biggest, just one that's around today.
Name it quietly in a few words, the way you'd name a bird you can see: this is the fear of not having enough. Then let the breath stay slow, and keep sitting; you don't have to fight it.

wordCard.voice: Mara comes. The god of desire and enemy of freedom shoots his flower arrow at the seated prince, and when it fails, calls up an army of horrors. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit and Pali: the name of the tempter in Buddhist stories, who tries to stop the awakening.

carryVoice: Your line: the bow of flowers. The soft pull comes before the army. Day seven hundred fifteen.
